L115: Conversely, any closed conic Lagrangian subvariety of the cotangent bundle arises like this [cite41†23 , Lemma 3]. So the map \(X\mapsto \Lambda _X\) induces an isomorphism
L116: $$\begin{aligned} {\mathscr {Z}}(W) = \{ \text {cycles on}\,W\} \;{\mathop {\longrightarrow }\limits ^{\sim }}\; {\mathscr {L}}(W) = \{ \text {conic Lagrangian cycles on}\,T^\vee W\}, \end{aligned}$$
L117: 
L118: where by a conic Lagrangian cycle we mean a \({\mathbb Z}\)-linear combination of closed conic Lagrangian subvarieties. In the case of projective varieties we can talk about the degree of conormal varieties:
L119: ### Definition 1.4
L120: 
L121: If W is projective, the degree homomorphism on conic Lagrangian cycles is the map
L122: 
L123: $$\begin{aligned} \deg : \quad {\mathscr {L}}(W) \;\longrightarrow \; \mathrm {CH}^n(T^\vee (W)) \;{\mathop {\longrightarrow }\limits ^{i^*}}\; \mathrm {CH}^n(W) \;\twoheadrightarrow \; {\mathbb Z}\end{aligned}$$
L124: 
L125: which is given by the intersection number with the zero section \(i: W \hookrightarrow T^\vee (W)\).
L126: ### Example 1.5
L127: 
L128: Over the complex numbers the above degree can be computed as follows. For any constructible function \(F: W\rightarrow {\mathbb Z}\) consider the topological Euler characteristic
L129: 
L130: $$\begin{aligned} \chi _\mathrm {top}(W, F) \;=\; \sum _{n\in {\mathbb Z}} \, n\cdot \chi _\mathrm {top}(F^{-1}(n)), \end{aligned}$$
L131: where \(\chi _\mathrm {top}(F^{-1}(n))\) denotes the alternating sum of the Betti numbers of \(F^{-1}(n)\). In the theory of characteristic classes of singular varieties this definition is applied to a particular constructible function \(\mathrm {Eu}_X: W \rightarrow {\mathbb Z}\), the local Euler obstruction of a subvariety \(X\subseteq W\) [cite42†29 , Sect. 3]. Outside of the singular locus \(\mathrm {Sing}(X)\subseteq X\) it has the form
L132: $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm {Eu}_X(p) \;=\; {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 &{} \text {for}\,p\in W{\setminus } X, \\ 1 &{} \text {for}\,p\in \mathrm {Sm}(X), \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
L133: 
L134: but its values on the singular locus depend on the singularities: For instance, if X is a curve, \(\mathrm {Eu}_X(p)\) is the multiplicity of that curve at p. In general, the degree of conormal varieties in Definition cite43†1.4 can be expressed as an Euler characteristic by the formula
L135: $$\begin{aligned} \deg (\Lambda _X) \;=\; (-1)^{\dim (X)} \cdot \chi _\mathrm {top}(X, \mathrm {Eu}_X), \end{aligned}$$
L136: see [cite40†34 , Lemme 1.2.1] [cite44†17 , Prop. 6.1(b)]. The right hand side can be computed easily as soon as we know the local Euler obstruction. For a smooth rational curve X we get \(\deg (\Lambda _X)=-2\) while a nodal or cuspidal cubic has \(\deg (\Lambda _X)=-3\). Note that a cuspidal cubic is homeomorphic to a smooth rational curve, so the degree of conormal varieties is not a topological invariant. Moreover, it can be negative.
L137: ### 1.4 Proof of the semicontinuity theorems
L138: 
L139: Of course there are no rational curves in abelian varieties, and in the case of abelian varieties the degree behaves much better. By [cite45†37 , Th. 1] we have the following result (see Sect. cite46†5 ):
L140: ### Proposition 1.6
L141: 
L142: If \(W=A\) is an abelian variety, then
L143: 
L144:   * \(\deg (\Lambda _X)\ge 0\) for any \(X\subset A\),
L145: 
L146:   * \(\deg (\Lambda _X)>0\) if and only if X is of general type,
L147: 
L148:   * \(\deg (\Lambda _X)=\deg (\gamma _X)\) for divisors \(X\subset A\) with Gauss map \(\gamma _X\).
L149: This easily implies Theorem cite33†1.1 when combined with the principle of Lagrangian specialization which we recall in sect. cite47†2 : For any flat family of subvarieties in a smooth ambient 1-parameter family, the limit of their conormal varieties is an effective conic Lagrangian cycle whose support contains the conormal variety to the central fiber as a component, and the total degree of the limit cycle equals the degree of a general fiber.
L150: The same argument shows that our semicontinuity result holds not only for divisors but for subvarieties of any codimension:
L151: ### Theorem 1.7
L152: 
L153: Let \(A \rightarrow S\) be an abelian scheme over a variety S, and let \(X\subset A\) be an arbitrary family of subvarieties which is flat over S. Then for each \(d\in {\mathbb N}\) the subsets \( S_d = \bigl \{ s\in S \mid \deg (\Lambda _{X_s}) \le d \bigr \} \subseteq S \) are closed in the Zariski topology.
L154: It remains to prove Theorem cite38†1.2 . Given the interpretation for the degree of Gauss maps in Proposition cite48†1.6 , the proof has nothing to do with abelian varieties: In Sect. cite49†3 we show that for any flat family of divisors on a smooth 1-parameter variety, the specialization of their conormal varieties contains an extra component whenever the singular locus of the fiber jumps.
L155: While the final criterion is phrased only for divisors, we formulate our arguments as far as possible for subvarieties in arbitrary codimension to get beyond Theorem cite38†1.2 (see Example cite50†3.6 ). This is important even if one only wants to study singularities of divisors: In the theory of Chern classes for singular varieties one attaches to any subvariety \(X\subset A\) a characteristic cycle of the form
L156: $$\begin{aligned} \Lambda \;=\; \Lambda _X + \sum _Z m_Z \Lambda _Z \end{aligned}$$
L157: 
L158: where Z runs through certain strata in \(\mathrm {Sing}(X)\) [cite41†23 , cite40†34 ], and the topologically meaningful invariant that appears in generalizations of the Gauss-Bonnet index formula is the total degree \(\deg (\Lambda )\) involving all the strata.
L159: ### 1.5 A topological view on jump loci
L160: In Sect. cite28†7 , which is not used in the rest of the paper, we deduce from our previous results a general semicontinuity theorem for the intersection cohomology of varieties over the complex numbers. Recall that for a complex variety X, the intersection cohomology \(\mathrm {IH}^\bullet (X)\) only depends on its homeomorphism type in the Euclidean topology; it coincides with Betti cohomology in the smooth case but is better behaved in general [cite51†6 , cite52†20 , cite53†21 , cite54†24 , cite55†30 ]. We denote by
L161: $$\begin{aligned} \chi _\mathrm {IC}(X) \;=\; \sum _{i\ge 0} \; (-1)^{i+\dim (X)} \dim \mathrm {IH}^i(X) \end{aligned}$$
L162: 
L163: the Euler characteristic of the intersection cohomology. This Euler characteristic is usually not semicontinuous in families, it can jump in both directions. But for families of finite branched covers of subvarieties in complex abelian varieties this does not happen (see Lemma cite56†7.6 and Corollary cite57†7.7 ):
L164: ### Theorem 1.8
L165: 
L166: Let \(f: X \rightarrow S\) be a family of varieties such that each fiber \(X_s\) is generically reduced and admits a finite morphism to an abelian variety. Then for each \(d\in {\mathbb N}_0\) the loci
L167: 
L168: $$\begin{aligned} S_d \;:=\; \{ s\in S \mid \chi _{\mathrm {IC}}(X_s) \le d \} \;\subseteq \; S \end{aligned}$$
L169: 
L170: are closed in the Zariski topology.
L171: This puts our results in a topological context, since the intersection cohomology of a complex variety only depends on its homeomorphism type. For instance, it follows from the above that a singular theta divisor cannot be homeomorphic to a smooth one (recall that there are examples of normal varieties which are singular but homemorphic to smooth varieties, such as those by Brieskorn [cite58†9 , cite59†10 ]).
L172: In Corollary cite60†7.9 we will see that the Jacobian locus appears in the stratification of \({\mathscr {A}}_g\) by the intersection cohomology of the theta divisor, so we obtain:
L173: ### Corollary 1.9
L174: 
L175: The locus of Jacobian varieties in \({\mathscr {A}}_g\) is an irreducible component of the closure of the locus of all ppav’s whose theta divisor is homeomorphic to a theta divisor on a Jacobian variety.
L176: 
L177: It seems an interesting problem to study the topology of theta divisors on abelian varieties in more detail.
L178: ## 2 Lagrangian specialization
L179: For convenience we include in this section a self-contained review of some basic facts about the specialization of Lagrangian cycles, which was introduced in relation with Chern–MacPherson classes [cite40†34 ] and nearby cycles for \({\mathscr {D}}\)-modules and perverse sheaves [cite39†19 ]. We work in a relative setting over a smooth curve S. The family of our ambient spaces is given by a smooth dominant morphism of varieties \(f:W\rightarrow S\) where \(\dim (W)=n+1\).
L180: Let \(X\subset W\) be a reduced closed subvariety. The relative smooth locus
L181: $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm {Sm}(X/S) \;=\; \{ \, x\in \mathrm {Sm}(X) \mid \; \text {the restriction}\, f|_X: X\rightarrow S\hbox { is smooth at }x \,\} \end{aligned}$$
L182: 
L183: is nonempty iff \(\dim f(X)>0\), in which case \(X\rightarrow S\) is flat and \(\mathrm {Sm}(X/S)\subset X\) is an open dense subset because \(\mathrm {char}(k)=0\). Any \(x\in \mathrm {Sm}(X/S)\) is a smooth point of the fiber \(X_{s} = f^{-1}(s)\cap X\) over the image point \(s=f(x)\). Hence inside the total space
L184: $$\begin{aligned} T^\vee (W/S) \;=\; T^\vee (W)/f^{-1}T^\vee (S) \end{aligned}$$
L185: 
L186: of the relative cotangent bundle, we define the relative conormal variety to X as the closure
L187: 
L188: $$\begin{aligned} \Lambda _{X/S} = \overline{\{ (x,\xi ) \in T^\vee (W/S) \mid x\in \mathrm {Sm}(X/S), \; \xi \perp T_x (X_{f(x)}) \}} \;\subset \; T^\vee (W/S). \end{aligned}$$
L189: ### Remark 2.1
L190: 
L191: In [cite61†8 ] the relative conormal variety is instead defined as the closure inside the absolute cotangent bundle. This notion of relative conormal variety is obtained from ours by base change via the quotient map \(T^\vee (W) \twoheadrightarrow T^\vee (W/S)\), i.e. we have
L192: 
L193: $$\begin{aligned} T^\vee (W) \times _{T^\vee (W/S)} \Lambda _{X/S} \;=\; \overline{ \{ (x,\xi ) \in T^\vee (W) \mid x\in \mathrm {Sm}(X/S), \; \xi \perp T_x X_{f(x)} \}}. \end{aligned}$$
L194: Indeed, both sides are irreducible closed subvarieties of \(T^\vee ( W)|_X\). For the right hand side this holds by definition, for the left hand side it follows from the fact that \(\Lambda _{X/S}\subset T^\vee (X/S)\) is an irreducible closed subvariety and \(T^\vee W\rightarrow T^\vee (X/S)\) is a fibration with irreducible fibers. So it suffices to show that both sides agree over some open dense \(U \subset X\).
L195: We can assume X is flat over S and take \(U=\mathrm {Sm}(X/S)\), in which case the claim becomes obvious.
L196: ### Lemma 2.2
L197: 
L198: If X is flat and irreducible over S, then so is \(\Lambda _{X/S}\).
L199: ### Proof
L200: 
L201: \(\Lambda _{X/S}\) is defined as the schematic closure of a locally closed subscheme V of the relative cotangent bundle \(T^\vee (A/S)\). The subscheme V is the total space of a vector bundle over a smooth variety, so it is a smooth variety as well. Its schematic closure is integral, and a morphism from an integral scheme to a smooth curve is flat iff it is dominant [cite62†22 , chapter III, Prop. 9.7]. \(\square \)
L202: Relative conormal varieties can be seen as families of conormal varieties. In what follows we denote by
L203: 
L204: $$\begin{aligned} {\mathscr {L}}(W/S) \;=\; \bigoplus _{X\subset W} {\mathbb Z}\cdot \Lambda _{X/S} \end{aligned}$$
L205: 
L206: the free abelian group on relative conormal varieties to closed subvarieties \(X\subset W\) that are flat over S. By the specialization of \(\Lambda \in {\mathscr {L}}(W/S)\) at \(s\in S(k)\) we mean the cycle
L207: $$\begin{aligned} {\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda ) \;=\; \bigl [ \Lambda \cdot f^{-1}(s) \bigr ] \end{aligned}$$
L208: 
L209: which underlies the schematic fiber of the morphism \(\Lambda _{X/S} \rightarrow S\) at s. This is again a conic Lagrangian cycle by the following classical result, see [cite63†18 , prop. (a), p. 179] or in an analytic setup [cite64†28 , Sect. 1.2]:
L210: ### Lemma 2.3
L211: 
L212: (Principle of Lagrangian specialization). The specialization at s gives a homomorphism
L213: 
L214: $$ {\mathrm {sp}}_s: \quad {\mathscr {L}}(W/S) \;\longrightarrow \; {\mathscr {L}}(W_s) $$
L215: 
L216: sending effective cycles to effective cycles. On Chow groups it induces the Gysin map in the bottom row of the following commutative diagram:
L217: 
L218: cite65†Image: figure a†media.springernature.com L219: 
L220: For any closed subvariety \(X\subset W\) which is flat over S, there is a finite subset \(\Sigma \subset S\) such that
L221: $$\begin{aligned} {\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S}) \;=\; {\left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \Lambda _{X_s} &{} \textit{for}\,\,\, s\in S{\setminus } \Sigma , \\ m_{X_s}\Lambda _{X_s} + \sum _{Z\subset \mathrm {Sing}(X_s)} m_{Z}\Lambda _Z &{} \textit{for} \,\,\, s\in \Sigma , \end{array}\right. } \end{aligned}$$
L222: 
L223: where \(m_{X_s}, m_{Z} > 0\) and the sum runs over finitely many subvarieties \(Z\subset \mathrm {Sing}(X_s)\).
L224: ### Proof
L225: 
L226: Note that \(T^\vee (W_s)\) is an effective Cartier divisor in \(T^\vee (W)\). It intersects properly any relative conormal variety to a subvariety which is flat over S. Hence it is clear that the specialization induces on Chow groups the Gysin map defined in [cite44†17 , Sect. 2.6] and sends effective cycles to effective cycles.
L227: Now take an irreducible subvariety \(X\subset W\) which is flat over S. By Lemma cite66†2.2 the morphism \(\Lambda _{X/S} \rightarrow S\) is flat and hence all its fibers are pure dimensional of the same dimension. Furthermore the action of the multiplicative group preserves the fibers of \(T^{\vee }(W/S)\rightarrow S\) and so the fibers of \(\Lambda _{X/S}\rightarrow S\) are unions of conic subvarieties.
L228: As the canonical relative symplectic form on \(T^{\vee }(W/S)\) restricts to the canonical symplectic form on \(T^{\vee }(W_s)\) for every s, we conclude that the fibers of \(\Lambda _{X/S}\rightarrow S\) are also Lagrangian and hence a union of conormal varieties, since the conic Lagrangian subvarieties of the cotangent bundle are precisely the conormal varieties [cite41†23 , Lemma 3]. The coefficients are non-negative as the specialization of effective cycles is effective.
L229: Hence \({\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S})\) is a sum of conormal varieties, and since under the morphism \(T^\vee (A_s) \rightarrow A_s\) its support surjects onto \(X_s\), we conclude that one of the appearing components must be \(\Lambda _{X_s}\).
L230: As \(\Lambda _{X/S}\) is irreducible and we work over a field of characteristic zero, there exists a Zariski open dense subset of S over which the fibers of the morphism \(\Lambda _{X/S}\rightarrow S\) are reduced and irreducible. We conclude that for s in this Zariski open dense subset of S we have \({\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S})=\Lambda _{X_s}\).
L231: Moreover, the specialization cannot have any further components over the relative smooth locus \(\mathrm {Sm}(X/S)\subseteq X\), since on that locus also the morphism \(\Lambda _{X/S}\rightarrow S\) restricts to a smooth morphism. \(\square \)
L232: We have the following consequence of flatness:
L233: ### Proposition 2.4
L234: 
L235: Let \(X\subset W\) be a closed subvariety which is flat over S, then the degree
L236: 
L237: $$\begin{aligned} d = \deg ({\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S})) \quad \hbox {is~independent~of~s}\in S(k). \end{aligned}$$
L238: ### Proof
L239: The cycle class of the specialization \({\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S})\) is the image of \([\Lambda _{X/S}]\) under the Gysin map in Lemma cite67†2.3 , and its degree is defined as the intersection number of this image with the zero section \( X=\mathcal {X} \hookrightarrow \mathcal {W} = T^\vee (W/S) \).
L240: As \(\mathcal {X}\) and \(\mathcal {W}\) are flat over S and \(\mathcal {X} \hookrightarrow \mathcal {W}\) is a regular embedding, the degree is therefore constant by [cite44†17 , Th. 10.2] applied to the relative conormal variety \(\mathcal {V}=\Lambda _{X/S}\). Note that \(\mathcal {V}\hookrightarrow \mathcal {W}\) is not required to be a regular embedding; in order to apply loc. cit. we only need that its base change to \(\mathcal {X}\) is proper over S, which is true. \(\square \)
L241: ### Remark 2.5
L242: For \(\mathrm {char}(k)>0\) the specialization of a family of conormal varieties need not be a sum of conormal varieties, see [cite68†25 , p. 215]. Similarly, for \(\mathrm {char}(k)=0\) we need \(\dim (S)=1\), otherwise we would have to restrict the class of morphisms as in [cite69†33 ].
L243: For instance, for \(S={\mathbb C}^2\ni s=(0,0)\) we have \(i_s^{-1}(\Lambda _{X/S}) = T^\vee (W/S)|_{X_s}\) for the subvariety \( X = \{ ((x,y,z), (x^2 - y^2 z, y)) \mid (x,y,z)\in {\mathbb C}^3 \} \subset W = {\mathbb C}^3 \times S. \)
L244: ## 3 Jump loci for the degree
L245: Let \(f: W\rightarrow S\) be a smooth dominant morphism from a smooth variety to a smooth curve as above. For any S-flat subvariety \(X\subset W\) and \(s\in S(k)\) we have seen that \( {\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S}) - \Lambda _{X_s} \ge 0, \) where the inequality means that the cycle on the left hand side is effective or zero. It is natural to ask for which \(s\in S(k)\) the above inequality is strict.
L246: In the notation of Lemma cite67†2.3 this happens iff \(m_Z > 0\) for some \(Z\subseteq \mathrm {Sing}(X_s)\). The following provides a sufficient criterion for this to happen for families of divisors:
L247: ### Proposition 3.1
L248: 
L249: Assume \(d=\mathrm {codim}(X, W)=1\). If \(\mathrm {Sing}(X/S)\) has an irreducible component which is contained in the fiber over some point \(s\in S(k)\), then for this component \(Z\subset X_s\) we have
L250: 
L251: $$\begin{aligned} {\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S})-\Lambda _{X_s} \; \ge \; \Lambda _Z. \end{aligned}$$
L252: We divide the proof in several steps. Most of the argument works in arbitrary codimension d, so for the moment we do not yet assume \(d=1\). It will be enough to prove the claim over some open dense subset of W metting Z. Fixing a general point \(p\in Z(k)\) and working locally near that point, we can assume that
L253: 
L254:   * \(Z=\mathrm {Sing}(X/S)\) (equality as a scheme),
L255: 
L256:   * \(T^\vee (W/S) \simeq W\times V\) is the trivial bundle with fiber \(V=T^\vee _p(W_s)\),
L257:   * \(X\subset W\) is cut out by a regular sequence \(f_1, \ldots , f_d \in H^0(W,\mathcal {O}_W)\).
L258: 
L259: By the first item each \(x\in (X{\setminus } Z)(k)\) is a smooth point of \(X_t\) for \(t=f(x)\). Fixing a trivialization as in the second item, we can furthermore identify the conormal space to \(X_t\subset W_t\) at x with a subspace in \(V= T^\vee _x(W_t)\) of codimension d. Consider the relative Gauss map
L260: 
L261: $$\begin{aligned} X{\setminus } Z \;\longrightarrow \; \hbox {Gr}(d, V ) \end{aligned}$$
L262: which sends each point to the corresponding conormal space. This is a rational map whose locus of indeterminacy is precisely Z. Let \(\gamma _X:\hat{X} \rightarrow \hbox {Gr}(d,V)\) denote its resolution of indeterminacy which is obtained by blowing up the base locus \(Z\subset X\) as in [cite44†17 , Sect. 4.4]:
L263: 
L264: cite70†Image: figure b†media.springernature.com L265: 
L266: We want to control the image of the exceptional divisor \(E_X=\pi _X^{-1}(Z) \subset \hat{X}\) under the map
L267: $$\begin{aligned} \alpha _X \;=\; (\pi _X, \gamma _X): \; \hat{X} \,\rightarrow \, X\times \hbox {Gr}(d, V) \,\subset \, W \times \hbox {Gr}(d, V) \;=\; \hbox {Gr}(d,T^\vee (W/S)). \end{aligned}$$
L268: ### Lemma 3.2
L269: 
L270: The morphism \(\alpha _X\) is a closed embedding.
L271: ### Proof
L272: 
L273: By assumption \(X\subset W\) is cut out by a regular sequence \(f_1, \dots , f_d\). The same then holds for each fiber \(X_t \subset W_t\). Hence it follows that the relative singular locus \(\mathrm {Sing}(X/S)\) is cut out as a closed subscheme of W by \(f_1, \dots , f_d\) and by the \(d\times d\) minors
L274: $$\begin{aligned} J(i_1, \dots , i_d) \;:=\; \det \begin{pmatrix} \partial _{i_1} (f_1) &{} \cdots &{} \partial _{i_1}(f_d) \\ \vdots &{} \ddots &{} \vdots \\ \partial _{i_d} (f_1) &{} \cdots &{} \partial _{i_d}(f_d) \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}$$
L275: 
L276: with \(1\le i_1< \cdots < i_d \le n\), where we fix an arbitrary basis \(\partial _1, \ldots , \partial _n \in V^\vee \) for the fiber of the relative tangent bundle and regard the basis vectors as relative derivations for the smooth morphism \(W\rightarrow S\).
L277: Now let \(\iota :X\times \hbox {Gr}(d, V)\hookrightarrow X\times \mathbb {P}(\Lambda ^d V )\) be the Plücker embedding of the Grassmannian as a closed subvariety of projective space. We want to show that the composite
L278: 
L279: $$\begin{aligned} \beta _X \;:=\; \iota \circ \alpha _X: \quad \hat{X} \;\longrightarrow \; X \times \hbox {Gr}(d, V) \longrightarrow X \times \mathbb {P}(\textstyle \bigwedge ^d V) \end{aligned}$$
L280: is a closed embedding. For this let \(I\unlhd \mathcal {O}_X\) be the ideal sheaf of \(Z\subset X\). Then we have
L281: 
L282: $$\begin{aligned} \hat{X} \;=\; {\mathrm {Proj}}_X R_I \quad \text {for the graded Rees algebra} \quad R_I \;:=\; \bigoplus _{n\ge 0} \; I^n \cdot t^n \;\subset \; {\mathscr {O}}_X[t], \end{aligned}$$
L283: 
L284: where t is a dummy variable to keep track of degrees. The homomorphism
L285: $$\begin{aligned} \beta _X^* :\quad \mathcal {O}_X\otimes \mathrm {Sym}^\bullet \left( \bigwedge ^{d}V^{\vee } \right) \;\longrightarrow \;\; R_I \;=\; \bigoplus _{n\ge 0} \; I^n \cdot t^n \end{aligned}$$
L286: 
L287: of graded \(\mathcal {O}_X\)-algebras satisfies
L288: 
L289: $$\begin{aligned} \beta _X^*(1\otimes (\partial _{i_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \partial _{i_d})) \;=\; J(i_1, \dots , i_d)|_X \cdot t \;\in \; I\cdot t \end{aligned}$$
L290: for \(1\le i_1< \cdots < i_k\le n\). But we have seen above that the \(\mathcal {O}_X\)-module I is generated by the minors on the right hand side. Hence it follows that \(\beta _X^*\) is an epimorphism in all degrees and so \(\beta _X\) is a closed immersion. \(\square \)
L291: ### Remark 3.3
L292: 
L293: If \(d=1\), then \(\hbox {Gr}(d, V)=\mathbb {P}V\) and the closed embedding \(\alpha _X\) induces an isomorphism
L294: 
L295: $$\begin{aligned} \alpha _X: \quad \hat{X} \;{\mathop {\longrightarrow }\limits ^{\sim }} \; \mathbb {P}\Lambda _{X/S}. \end{aligned}$$
L296: Indeed, the blowup \(\hat{X}\) is again reduced and irreducible by [cite62†22 , II.7.16]. Via \(\alpha _X\) it is therefore an integral closed subscheme of \(W\times \mathbb {P}V\) and as such it can be recovered as the Zariski closure of its restriction over the open dense subset \(S{\setminus } \{s\}\subset S\), where it coincides with \(\mathbb {P}\Lambda _{X/S}\subset W\times \mathbb {P}V\) by definition.
L297: In particular, one may look at the scheme-theoretic fiber of \(\hat{X}\) over \(s\in S(k)\) to compute the multiplicities in \({\mathrm {sp}}_s(\Lambda _{X/S})\). For \(d>1\) the situation becomes more complicated, so in what follows we restrict ourselves to set-theoretic arguments. To pass back to conormal varieties we look at the projection \( \hbox {Fl}(d, 1, V) \longrightarrow \hbox {Gr}(d, V) \) from the partial flag variety.
L298: This projection is a smooth equidimensional morphism of relative dimension \(d-1\). On the fiber product \(Y = \hat{X} \times _{\hbox {Gr}(d, V)} \hbox {Fl}(d,1,V)\) consider the morphism
L299: $$\begin{aligned} \alpha _Y = (\pi _Y, \gamma _Y): \quad Y \;\longrightarrow \; X\times \mathbb {P}V \end{aligned}$$
